precepts.text: The saints are those that made a covenant with the Most High by sacrifice, the Israelites who came out of Egypt.
precepts.point: This punishment will not last forever. His anger endures but a moment and His favor is life; weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning. What feels like eternity to us is a little time to the Most High.

note.label: Psalm 30: Joy Cometh in the Morning

precepts.why:
“Sing unto the Lord, O ye saints of his, and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness.” He specifies His saints, and Psalm 50 says who they are: “Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.”

The saints are those that made a covenant with the Most High by sacrifice, the Israelites who came out of Egypt. It is those saints who are told to sing, because this punishment will not last forever: His anger endures but a moment, weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning. What feels like eternity to us is a little time to the Most High.

precepts.text: In the day of prosperity there is forgetfulness of affliction, and in the day of affliction no more remembrance of prosperity; people forget to save and prepare when things go well, and forget past prosperity when things go wrong.
precepts.point: In my prosperity I said I shall never be moved: the key point of making the Most High your refuge and salvation is staying on the right path regardless, whether prosperity or affliction comes.

note.label: Psalm 30: Joy Cometh in the Morning

precepts.why:
“And in my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved.” Ecclesiasticus shows what prosperity does to the mind: “In the day of prosperity there is a forgetfulness of affliction: and in the day of affliction there is no more remembrance of prosperity.”

People forget to save and prepare when things go well, and forget past prosperity when things go wrong. The key point of making the Most High your refuge and salvation is staying on the right path regardless, whether prosperity or affliction comes.

precepts.text: If you come to serve the Most High, prepare your soul, set your heart right, endure, and take whatever is brought upon you cheerfully, staying patient when changed to a lower state.
precepts.point: In my prosperity I said I shall never be moved: the key point of making the Most High your refuge and salvation is staying on the right path regardless, whether prosperity or affliction comes.

note.label: Psalm 30: Joy Cometh in the Morning

precepts.why:
Prosperity says, I shall never be moved, but the one who serves the Most High is told to get ready: “My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation. Set thy heart aright, and constantly endure, and make not haste in time of trouble.”

“Cleave unto him, and depart not away, that thou mayest be increased at thy last end. Whatsoever is brought upon thee take cheerfully, and be patient when thou art changed to a low estate.” If you come to serve the Most High, prepare your soul, set your heart right, endure, and take whatever is brought upon you cheerfully, staying patient when changed to a lower state. That is staying on the right path regardless, whether prosperity or affliction comes.

precepts.text: In captivity, repent and make supplication saying we have sinned and committed wickedness; then He hears the prayer and maintains our cause. He only hears when we repent.
precepts.point: To make supplication is to plead, ask forgiveness, and confess specifically what we have done. You cannot just say "Lord I have sinned"; you must name what you are dealing with.

note.label: Psalm 30: Joy Cometh in the Morning

precepts.why:
“I cried to thee, O Lord; and unto the Lord I made supplication.” To make supplication is to plead, ask forgiveness, and confess specifically what we have done. Solomon shows how it is done in captivity: “Yet if they shall bethink themselves in the land whither they were carried captives, and repent, and make supplication unto thee in the land of them that carried them captives, saying, We have sinned, and have done perversely, we have committed wickedness”.

You cannot just say "Lord I have sinned"; you must name what you are dealing with: we have sinned, done perversely, committed wickedness. “And so return unto thee with all their heart, and with all their soul, in the land of their enemies, which led them away captive, and pray unto thee toward their land, which thou gavest unto their fathers”.

“Then hear thou their prayer and their supplication in heaven thy dwelling place, and maintain their cause”. When we repent and make supplication in captivity, He hears the prayer and maintains our cause. He only hears when we repent; that is why He hid His face and David was troubled, and why David cried and made supplication.

precepts.text: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper, but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy; hide your sins and you will be buried by them.
precepts.point: Prayer is largely invalid if there is no action behind it. If you ask for a home but take no steps toward the finances, why would you receive it. Faith without works is dead.

note.label: Psalm 30: Joy Cometh in the Morning

precepts.why:
David asks “What profit is there in my blood, when I go down to the pit? Shall the dust praise thee?” and then “Hear, O Lord, and have mercy upon me: Lord, be thou my helper.” Solomon shows how that mercy comes: “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.” Hide your sins and you will be buried by them.

That is why repenting daily means naming the sin specifically. The Most High looks for us to say exactly what we are dealing with. One brother may struggle with fornication, another with cigarettes; you cannot bring the same prayer for both, so make it clearly known what you are dealing with, the way you would tell your mother or father exactly what you need, not just asking the Lord to bless you. Confess it, then forsake it, and the mercy David prayed for comes.

precepts.text: Salvation belongeth unto the Most High; affirmed as a precept for Psalms 27:1 on the Most High being salvation.
precepts.point: Prayer is largely invalid if there is no action behind it. If you ask for a home but take no steps toward the finances, why would you receive it. Faith without works is dead.

note.label: Psalm 30: Joy Cometh in the Morning

precepts.why:
“Salvation belongeth unto the Lord: thy blessing is upon thy people.” When David cries “Lord, be thou my helper”, he knows where the help comes from. The Most High is salvation, the same understanding given for Psalms 27:1, and his blessing is upon his people.

He turned David's “mourning into dancing”, put off his sackcloth and “girded me with gladness”, “To the end that my glory may sing praise to thee, and not be silent.” That is the kingdom, where we will sing thanks to the Most High for ever.

But salvation belonging to the Lord does not make us idle. As Israelites we seek a country, the kingdom and this world back, and we must make that request known plainly. And prayer is largely invalid if there is no action behind it: if you ask for a home but take no steps toward the finances, why would you receive it? Faith without works is dead.

precepts.text: This is the book of the Commandments; the whole book is the law, so there is no single list. Those that keep it come to life, but such as leave it shall die.
precepts.point: Prayer is largely invalid if there is no action behind it. If you ask for a home but take no steps toward the finances, why would you receive it. Faith without works is dead.

note.label: Psalm 30: Joy Cometh in the Morning

precepts.why:
“O Lord my God, I will give thanks unto thee for ever.” We will sing thanks to the Most High for ever in the kingdom, but only if we do what we are supposed to do. Baruch shows what that is: “This is the book of the commandments of God, and the law that endureth for ever: all they that keep it shall come to life; but such as leave it shall die.”

The whole book is the law, so there is no single list to check off. Those that keep it come to life, the life David looks to when he asks whether the dust can praise the Most High or declare his truth; such as leave it shall die. Keeping the book is the action behind the prayer, and without that action the prayer is largely invalid.
